stories.title: Rams were right to not wait for 2027 QB class
stories.summary: Projecting “next year’s” QB class is an exercise in permanent uncertainty
stories.detailText: The Los Angeles Rams drafted quarterback Ty Simpson with the 13th overall pick this year and that was probably higher than any other team would have taken the inexperienced Alabama signal-caller, but the reason Les Snead did it was: Opportunity. The Rams didn’t expect to have a high first-round pick in 2027 — they would later trade it for Myles Garrett anyway — and Simpson was the best available of a weak bunch. Some argued that even the sixth or seventh-best quarterback in 2027 would be a better prospect than Simpson. A “historic” class, they said. Arch you sure about that? Because Manning, I’ve got some news for you … For most of 2023 to 2025, the media and many fans were practically desperate to proclaim that Arch Manning would become the next great NFL quarterback, anointing him as a future number one overall pick even before he enrolled at Texas as the top prospect in the country. Manning’s star was so bright that it also shone a light on many other quarterbacks expected to be available in the 2027 class, some of whom would be first-time eligible and others who returned to college for more NIL money. Dante Moore, C.J. Carr, Drew Mestemaker, LaNorris Sellers, Trinidad Chambliss, Darian Mensah, Julian Sayin, and Jayden Maiava to name eight. ESPN’s Jordan Reid recently posted a big board in which he had zero quarterbacks in the top-7, until Mestemaker lands at eight, and then there isn’t another QB until Chambliss at 15. There are just three QBs in the top-20 and Manning is now being projected to go back to school for a fifth season — perhaps not at Texas. NEW: Arch Manning took significantly fewer first-team reps with Texas’ first-team offense this week than he typically does, ESPN reports. Backup KJ Lacey Jr. had a precipitous uptick in first-team reps. https://t.co/jx1sPSqDOH pic.twitter.com/zF4APo9SYj — On3 (@On3) October 24, 2026 2027 Mock Drafts were eager to put five or six quarterbacks in the top-10 — to a sickening degree — and to argue that the entire landscape of the league could be altered by the “Manning Class”. At worst, the 2027 draft should resemble classes in 2018, 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024, when quarterbacks were heavily concentrated in the top-5 or top-12 picks. I mean, right there are five recent classes that had at least three quarterbacks get drafted immediately, and 2027 was being cited as better than ALL of them. But two months into the college season, the Manning Class looks more like a Clowning Class. By getting to spend 2026 with Ty Simpson, giving him an extra year of development and NFL coaching, did the Rams actually get a better quarterback prospect than anyone they could have had in 2027? What went wrong with Arch and company? If you are like me and you have always said that Arch Manning is the most overrated prospect of the century, please leave a comment below so I know I’m not alone on this hill. I know I wasn’t, but it was hard to get a word in like “But…. why? ” when you’ve got practically every draft analyst in the industry making excuses for Manning and telling us we didn’t “know ball” because not all of us were ready to call him a future first-round pick. He has never done anything on a football field that suggests he’s a first-round pick, let alone first overall. Yet you had everyone from Todd McShay to Mel Kiper to Field Yates arguing the opposite. Maybe they’d bring up ONE play or ONE trait, but at the end of the day if his name was “Arch Munning” we wouldn’t even know about him. (Except maybe to giggle that there’s a QB named “Munning”.) "I'll go with the Oregon quarterback over Arch [Manning]. I'll go Dante Moore." @MoveTheSticks believes that Oregon's Dante Moore can be the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NFL draft 👀 (via @RichEisenShow ) pic.twitter.com/iFujfzIdJB — NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) April 27, 2026 This rant is not about Arch Manning, it’s about the media/draft ecosystem that allows analysts to spread misinformation about a prospect for clicks, views, or simply out of peer pressure. The Internet is not a welcoming place for dissenting views, let’s be honest. Here’s a very brief Manning timeline: He dominated high schoolers in 2A division class with no other real Division I prospects Even then, Manning’s team would lose badly in the playoffs every year (an elite QB should be enough under those circumstances) He sat as a true freshman—which is fine He sat as a sophomore too—which is not fine, especially when the starter is Quinn Ewers In his third year with Steve Sarkisian, he starts his career throwing five picks in five games Including picks against UTEP and San Jose State Manning got praised for finishing strong in 2025, but even at the end of the year he averaged under 7 yards per attempt and he was supposed to be surrounded by one of the best teams in the country. Although Arch Manning may have gotten drafted over Fernando Mendoza this year — maybe — did he go back to school for more seasoning or did he go back because he heard from the NFL that he wouldn’t go as high as everyone expected? Because to the Mannings, it would be embarrassing if Arch had all this hype and wasn’t drafted top-5, top-10, or even ahead of Ty Simpson. Ty Simpson was a better player than Arch Manning in 2025, after all. Better by a lot. Having now lost back-to-back games against unranked opponents, Texas is considering benching Manning for a true freshman. According to Tom Pelissero, he texted someone familiar with Manning and was told that it’s more likely that Manning is at Ole Miss next season than he is in the NFL Draft. “I texted one person who’s known Arch (Manning) a long time earlier tonight, and I said, ‘Where do you see Arch in 2027?’ And his response was Ole Miss.” — @TomPelissero on the latest Bill Simmons Podcast Manning and Texas will host Ole Miss this weekend. — Josh Ward (@Josh_Ward) October 23, 2026 To some people these developments are shocking. To some of us, it was apparent as soon as Manning spent a second year behind Ewers that something was wrong with this picture. Manning isn’t the only Faller Daniel Jeremiah and many others claimed that actually Dante Moore was the elite future MVP candidate in the 2027 QB Class. But Moore suffered a serious head injury against USC and will miss his third straight game. Oregon QB Dante Moore has been ruled OUT for Saturday’s game vs. Illinois. Moore will miss his third straight game as he continues to recover from a concussion. pic.twitter.com/yjsb68ANzz — Yahoo Sports (@YahooSports) October 22, 2026 Moore is now just 37th on Reid’s big board. Some see C.J. Carr as the best prospect in the draft. Despite an impressive TD/INT ratio of 16:1, Carr is seen as merely having average traits and being a borderline first-round pick , not a lock. Tested against the BYU defense last week, Carr was held to just 261 yards and no touchdowns on 49 passes as Notre Dame lost for the first time. It seems like every year someone is saying that LaNorris Sellers is about to prove he’s the next Lamar Jackson. But he’s a career 63% passer, throws too many picks, and hasn’t come anywhere close to Lamar’s rushing stats. Julian Sayin was supposed to be the next great Ohio State quarterback who would go into the draft as a top pick. But unimpressive physical traits never matched his Buckeyes-juiced stats and now he’s out indefinitely with an arm injury. Ohio State coach Ryan Day said that QB Julian Sayin is out indefinitely. There’s a plan being put in place for Sayin not being available for both the regular season and postseason. He said there’s no specific timeline on the recovery. He’s dealing with an injury on his throwing… pic.twitter.com/b3AZ669S21 — Pete Thamel (@PeteThamel) October 20, 2026 Instead, many mock drafters have turned to Oklahoma State’s Drew Mestemaker as the last hope of the 2027 draft. But not even Mestemaker is getting projected as the number one pick. That’s almost always Ohio State receiver Jeremiah Smith now. Reid cites Mestemaker’s quick ascension as an inexperienced starter who has already become one of the best passers in the country: Mestemaker is my top quarterback prospect despite this being only his second season as a starter in high school and college. He has an unconventional style, holding the ball at his waistline before ripping a fiery, three-quarters release. Mestemaker has the confidence to test the tightest of windows from various platforms, but that can get the best of him and lead to turnovers. Plus, he can be oblivious to underneath defenders. Mestemaker is bit of a streaky passer, though his hot streaks feature plenty of “wow” moments. And he is capable of being a running threat. But Mestemaker already has six picks in six games. Next up is Chambliss and Mensah. Neither of them would seem to be anything close to a top-three pick. They might not sniff the top-10. So with the 2026 class only featuring two first-round quarterbacks — Mendoza at 1 and Simpson at 13 — could it actually end up stronger than 2027? You’ll still find plenty of mock drafts that have Mestemaker, Mensah, and Carr in the top-10. Maybe it will shake out that way. Maybe five quarterbacks will go in the first-round after all, if not more. (If not Moore.) But that narrative sure has shifted dramatically since the offseason: “The 2027 QB class is historically great” to “The 2027 QB class … Uhh… it could still be … well … you don’t know! You can’t predict the future!” Yeah. Apparently nobody can.

stories.title: Stock up, stock down from Northwestern’s explosive 42-14 defeat of Rutgers
stories.summary: Explosiveness on both sides of the ball carries the ‘Cats to their sixth win.
stories.detailText: EVANSTON, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 24: Aidan Chiles #0 of the Northwestern Wildcats celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the first half against the Rutgers Scarlet Knights at Ryan Field on October 24, 2026 in Evanston, Illinois. (Photo by Jayden Mack/Getty Images) | Getty Images A triumphant victory for the Wildcats. From start to finish, Northwestern kept the pedal to the metal on the Scarlet Knights, hopping out to a quick 21-3 lead and holding onto that margin the rest of the way. It’s another Big Ten win for the ‘Cats, one that adds to its College Football Playoff campaign, which continued to grow in odds following Texas Tech’s loss to Cincinnati in the morning slate. Here are the biggest trends from the purple jerseys’ Saturday win: Stock up Pass rush The big boys got after Rutgers’ signal-callers. On its second drive of the game, Michael Kilbane got after AJ Surace, strip-sacking him at the Rutgers 8-yard line. Jamaal Johnson would recover the fumble, setting up Honig’s eight-yard touchdown reception two plays later. And in the third quarter, as Rutgers mounted some offensive momentum, it was the pass rush that stood tall defending the end zone. Linebacker Kobie McKinzie brought down Ashenfelder for a fourth-and-7 stop on its own 7-yard line and in the fourth quarter an NU pass rush contributed to errant throws from Ashenfelder on two fourth downs in NU territory, one of which resulted in a Jalen Lewis interception. Led by McKinzie, who had a sack, a TFL and a quarterback hit, and Kilbane, who had a sack and a TFL, Northwestern’s quarterback hunters finished with four sacks, five tackles for loss and five quarterback hits, good for their best performance of the season. With the Wildcats still down a couple players in the secondary, the capability NU showed Saturday to dial up some heat with a four-man rush could be critical to whether it has success late in the season. Explosive rushing EXPLOSIVE ON THE GROUND! The ‘Cats finished with nine explosive running plays (gains of 10 or more yards), four of which were good for 30+ yards. Three of the big gains came from Caleb Komolafe, who ripped off a 30-yard gain on the ‘Cats’ first touchdown drive, a 56-yard gain on the ‘Cats’ second touchdown drive and a 33-yard touchdown run late in the second quarter to put NU up 28-3. Komolafe finished the first half with six carries for 121 yards, and concluded the game with 150 yards on 11.5 yards per carry. Aidan Chiles was also extremely efficient as a runner, continuing to showcase his mobility as a game-changing attribute. Chiles posted his CAREER HIGH in rushing yards against the Scarlet Knights, taking a quarterback keeper to the house for a 37-yard touchdown run and finishing the game with 12 carries for 83 yards. Northwestern finished the game with 6.9 rushing efficiency and 283 yards — its second highest rushing total of the season. The ‘Cats are now averaging 204.6 yards per game, which before Saturday would have been good in the Big Ten standings for second in the Big Ten. The Sioux Falls route runner How about Griffin Wilde? Wilde continues to turn the heads of more and more NFL draft scouts, asserting himself game after game as one of college football’s most reliable pass catchers and purest route runners. The senior hit the ground running early, hauling in two third-down receptions on the ‘Cats’ first possession of the game before making a 13-yard touchdown reception to punctuate his hot start. Then, after quieting down for the rest of the first quarter, Wilde made 25+ yard receptions on each of the ‘Cats’ first two drives in the second period, pushing himself over 100 yards on the game with over nine minutes remaining in the half. Wilde finished the game with nine receptions, 133 yards and a touchdown. The senior is now averaging 87.9 yards per game this season and has an average yards per reception of 15.8 yards. Not to mention, he still hasn’t dropped a pass. Last year Wilde was good, but this year he has been great, becoming one of the Big Ten’s best. Honorable mentions: Red zone offense, Chiles making plays off schedule Stock down Run defense With 1:46 remaining in the second half, the game had been completely dominated by Northwestern. Rutgers had mounted just one scoring drive, and on its last four drives it had three punts — two of which were off three-and-outs — and a fumble. The ‘Cats were up 28-3, completely in the driver’s seat… and then their run defense collapsed. On its second drive of the third quarter, Rutgers marched right down the field without throwing a single pass, gashing the field open with 83 rushing yards on five carries. Then, after Chiles threw his first interception of the season, Raymond ripped off a 46-yard touchdown run on the second play of Rutgers’ subsequent drive, putting the Scarlet Knights in the end zone for the only time all day. Rutgers finished the game with 244 rushing yards on 6.3 efficiency. Plain and simple, in the final thirty minutes of the game, Northwestern had little answer for Antwan Raymond and the scarlet rushing attack. There’s no doubt the ‘Cats missed their second-leading tackler Robert Fitzgerald, but the real concern here is that this isn’t a game-specific issue. It’s not an overstatement to say that the ‘Cats would be undefeated if not for its run defense, which allowed 271 yards on 40 carries against Indiana, including three carries of 30 or more yards. The ‘Cats also allowed 147 rushing yards against South Dakota State and 180 yards against Colorado, including an explosive 35-yard rushing touchdown. Tim McGarigle will need to find a way to stop the run if Northwestern wants to keep winning games. Controllable mistakes Despite Northwestern’s dominance in this football game, there is still some room for criticism. As has been the case in many of its games this season, some of NU’s most negative drive results were completely self-inflicted. With 11:35 remaining in the second quarter, Jackson Kleather missed a 47-yard field goal try. While Kleather was praised following his clutch game-winner against MSU, the senior transfer is now 3-for-6 on field goal attempts of over 40 yards — those are points lost that are self-caused. Then, near the end of the half, a 15-yard roughing-the-passer penalty on senior linebacker Matthew Smith set Rutgers up in NU territory, leading to its 35-yard field goal as time expired in the period. Sure, the Scarlet Knights also supported that drive with 43 other yards, but the drive was kickstarted by the Smith penalty. On Saturday, the ‘Cats were dominant enough elsewhere that these plays didn’t affect the outcome of the game. However, in games against stronger opponents, Northwestern may not be afforded the same security. In its upcoming games against Oregon, No. 15 Iowa and No. 3 Ohio State, it would be a tragic feeling if a late game roughing-the-passer penalty or missed field goal ended up being the difference in a critical game. Honorable mentions: Aidan Chiles’ turnover rate after throwing his first interception of the season, half of the student section leaving after halftime

stories.detailText: (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens will be without Lamar Jackson for the third consecutive week, as the quarterback continues working his way back from a high-ankle sprain he suffered back in Week 4 against the Tennessee Titans. Jackson returned to practice earlier this week, for the first time since suffering the injury in the second half against Tennessee, but has been officially ruled out by the Ravens ahead of Sunday’s clash with their AFC North rivals the Cincinnati Bengals. After practicing this week, Jackson spoke with the media about the injury : “I just know it was a sprain, and it hurt bad,” Jackson said as quoted by the official Ravens website. “It was very, very, very, very, very painful. “Just trying to move how I move,” Jackson said. “If I can’t do that, I can’t help my team. I can’t put my team in a situation to win. I feel like I’m doing a disservice, if anything.” Tyler Huntley stepped in for Jackson against Tennessee, and led the Ravens to an overtime win over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 5. While Huntley was fairly sharp against Atlanta, completing 24-of-32 passes for 201 yards and a pair of touchdowns in the 30-23 win, he completed just 19-of-31 passes for 165 yards and a touchdown as the Ravens lost to the Cleveland Browns in Week 6.

stories.detailText: Sep 27, 2026; Denver, Colorado, USA; Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix (10) celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Los Angeles Rams during the second half at Empower Field at Mile High. Mandatory Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect It seems like a long time ago we were reading a UFG and watching the Broncos (because 10 days is an eternity in an NFL season!) but we are back and ready to see this team kick it into another gear after some time off and a slightly easier opponent. Kingbronco58 is back to show us how the Broncos’ offense can take charge for four quarters (looking at you, Payton), what Nix needs to do, and how the defense can continue to make life miserable for opponents. Kingbronco58 is one of our younger fans (who I met at a Broncos Raiders game years ago!) who joined the flock in the McDaniels era, which I always have to point out because it’s a little amazing he stuck around! But I’m so glad he did, and his Broncos Mount Rushmore is a testament to his fandom (now if he’ll just go watch those old Elway games too!!) "I’m confident in myself. I know I’m going to get back and be exactly what I was, if not better because as I’ve got older, that’s how it’s been. My training is going like this (points up) and at the end of the day, it’s all about getting better” —Bo Nix https://t.co/1KyOrDZ4UT — Zac Stevens (@ZacStevens) October 23, 2026 Week 7: Broncos at Cardinals MHR – It’s been a while since the OT win over the Seahawks. Quick thoughts on that second-half collapse, but OT save for the W? Kingbronco58: I think the second half collapse just speaks to the second half adjustments made by Mike McDonald and a talented Seahawks defense. With the way the game started, I thought we were finally about to see the offense put together a complete game. Hopefully this week, we finally get to see it come together. But at the end of the day we escaped a gauntlet of six games with a 4-2 record, and I think most would have been happy with 3-3 before the season. MHR – Ironically, this question was from last year’s Week 7 game… but it’s sadly appropriate again this season! The “offense struggles, defense saves the day” is a common theme. How frustrating is it that by Week 7 Bo Nix and the offense are still (and once again) mostly relying on the defense to “get” the win? Or should we be cool with having such a strong defense? Kingbronco58: It’s definitely frustrating that we are seeing it again, especially when we added Waddle in the offseason thinking he’d help the offense take the next step. I personally think this is still largely tied to Bo not mentally over the hurdle of his playoff injury. Theres been a ton of chatter on Twitter about how the Broncos need to move on from Bo after two years of slow starts. We’ve seen Bo go toe to toe with some of the best QBs in the league after starting slow. I’d rather see him peak in the playoffs when it matters than disappear when it matters. Having a strong defense that can carry when the offense is finding its footing is a luxury many teams would love to have, so I don’t see any reason that wouldn’t be cool. MHR – The Broncos offense also falls into a familiar pattern – very few yards on 1st and 2nd down, creating 3rd and long which always brings a lot of pressure and usually leads to a three-an-out. In general terms, what is holding this team back? Or is it just playing really good defenses? Kingbronco58: I feel like the offense struggling has been for a variety of reasons. We generally do a poor job challenging the middle of the field on the passing game. Wide receivers drop too many balls. No one consistently gets open. Dobbins has looked awful to start the season and the run game has been inefficient. And our play calling lacks creativity. Do all of these need to be fixed before the offense gets back on track? I don’t think so. But we need to see improvements in a lot of areas, playing really good defenses obviously doesn’t help when we are already struggling. But for the second year in a row we see the offense show up in plenty of games in the second half. MHR – Will we ever see the Jaylen Waddle we were promised? Kingbronco58: I really hope so, I can’t tell where the disconnect is with Waddle. But having traded a first round pick for him, his performance thus far is disappointing as fan and as a fantasy football owner. MHR – Bo Nix has acknowledged he needs to play better, and Sean Payton has taken some responsibility for the offensive struggles. Are you concerned about Nix’s performance overall? Any worry about the long-term projection for Nix as the franchise QB? Kingbronco58: I’m a little concerned, but we saw this last year as well. I feel like he’s playing not to lose instead playing to win while also struggling to overcome the mental aspects of his injury. He still has shown some flashes, like the Jacksonville game, and even the second half of the Rams game. I’m not rushing to make any decisions on Nix as the franchise QB yet. The reality is we are just now in year 3. We have the 5th year option and a franchise tag before we are absolutely locked into Nix as the franchise guy. A year ago Texans fans were having the same conversation, asking if Stroud was done after having a down year. And Stroud has really bounced back this year, so lets not rush into trying to draft another QB because Nix has struggled so far this year. For what its worth, I still Bo-lieve. This is for you, @Broncos fans: Evan Williams says his former Oregon teammate Bo Nix will be back STRONGER THAN EVER 💪 @evan_williams32 | @heykayadams pic.twitter.com/mfDXYlRHwG — Up & Adams (@UpAndAdamsShow) October 23, 2026 MHR – The Cardinals’ defense has struggled overall, but Budda Baker remains one of the league’s most versatile defensive backs, recording 42 tackles, 3.5 sacks and an interception this season. If he ends up playing, how concerned are you that Baker will be a big disrupter for an already inconsistent offense? And even if he’s out, how do you think the offense will handle Arizona’s tendency to disguise its defensive looks? Kingbronco58: I guess to an extent I’m not that worried about a specific guy or disguised defenses. I’m sure this response will come back to bite me. The Broncos have already played some really good defenses, including teams that have coordinators that like to disguise defensive looks. I think this is the easiest matchup of the season so far; if the offense struggles again I don’t think they deserve any excuses. MHR – The Broncos’ running game has struggled to establish much consistency, but Arizona has been one of the league’s worst teams defending the run. Is this finally the week Denver gets its ground game going? And which running back do you think should and could carry the load? If Jonah Coleman is back, does that change anything? Kingbronco58: I don’t think the run game gets going this week unless the Broncos have a big lead. The O-line hasn’t been consistent opening up holes in the run game this season. I want to see Harvey get more carries. We all know that he’s extremely good in the passing game, but not getting him carries telegraphs what the offense is going to do. I think Dobbins carries the load again this week, but it wouldn’t surprise me if Coleman becomes the guy as we get later into the season. I expect Coleman to play this week but after a month off, I don’t see a drastic improvement in the run game as he will be eased into playing time. MHR – This is game three with Sean Payton calling plays. Do you think the switch was a good choice? How would you grade his play-calling the last two games? What would you like to see improved and what specifically do you think should be Payton’s emphasis this week when it comes to passing plays, run/pass balance, creativity, etc.? Kingbronco58: I think the switch happened too early. The stats say that Davis Webb’s offense looked just slightly better than what we’ve seen from Payton. That said, I think Payton has done a better job staying balanced and sticking to an inefficient run game than Webb had. I would give Payton a C in play calling after his first two games. It feels like he still gets overly conservative at times. I’d like to see us do two things better. One, I want to see us attack the middle of the field more. Looking at Bo’s passing charts everything is to the outside, but Bo is very good passing to the middle of the field. He just doesn’t do it often for some reason, I’d like to see that change. Two, I want to see more schemed targets for both Sutton and Waddle. Both our WRs are off to slow starts this season, so let’s get them touches early and get them involved in the game. This week I want to see Payton go for the jugular. I don’t really care if that means Bo throws 55 times or we run the ball a ton. But I’m tired of getting the lead and just trying to milk the clock away like we kind of did against the Seahawks. MHR – Jonathon Cooper will be back this Sunday. Will his presence make a big difference? How do you think Que Robinson and Jonah Elliss have done in his place the last six games? What will it do for Nik Bonitto? Kingbronco58: I think his presence will make an impact. He’s a better run defender than Que and still a good pass rusher. We’ve seen this defense struggle a bit with the run, so having Cooper set the edge is hopefully helpful. I think Que and Jonah have both shown flashes stepping in for Cooper. Que especially has shown some terrific pass rush ability. I think this opens up the opportunity for Bonitto to be the sack artist we saw last year as there is a more respected threat on the other side. The bigger advantage in my opinion is it helps the whole pass rush stay fresher by having another option in the rotation. MHR – Trey McBride is arguably Arizona’s biggest offensive weapon, leading the NFL with 49 receptions through six games. Denver’s defense has generally done a good job limiting opponents’ top receiving threats, but not always so good with the TEs. How would you approach defending him, and how much does Patrick Surtain II’s potential availability change that strategy? Kingbronco58: TEs always feel like they are the bane of Vance Joseph’s defenses, I don’t expect that to change this week ( *editor’s note: bonus points for using “bane” in a sentence!) McBride is an extremely talented TE and practically the only weapon that the Cardinals have. I expect him to get his targets and have a solid to good game. I would always double team him, though. Make someone else on the team beat us. I don’t think Surtain plays this week, but if he did I don’t think it would change the strategy of containing McBride significantly. MHR – Ja’Quan McMillian is having an outstanding year. What do you like best about his game and do you think Vance Joseph should use him more? Kingbronco58: Ja’Quan McMillian reminds me a lot of Chris Harris. There is nearly nothing McMillian cannot do from the slot. He’s a very timely blitzer, and does a great job covering the player he’s across from. He also is willing to take chances to go for the turnover. I think Vance would be dumb to not use him as much as he can because he’s such a versatile player. Ja'Quan McMillian has the second-most TFLs among CBs in Broncos history. Ja'Quan (18) only trails Chris Harris Jr (23). He has more than Champ Bailey (13). — Zac Stevens (@ZacStevens) October 23, 2026 MHR – Arizona is just 2-4, but the Cardinals are coming off an impressive 18-16 upset of the Rams. What concerns you most about this Cardinals team, and what did they show against LA that should have Denver fans paying attention? Kingbronco58: They won that game kicking six field goals, and nearly lost it at the very end. I think divisional matchups can always get a little weird given how familiar the two teams are. I think what was most impressive about their game against LA was how they moved the ball even if they struggled to punch it into the end zone. The offense was consistently driving and having a chance to put points on the board. McBride is my biggest concern about the Cardinals, but I covered how to handle him! MHR – Denver’s defense continues to be the backbone of this team, and Zach Allen is its main support. Going against his former team, how big of a factor do you expect Allen to be in the pass rush specifically and the potential defensive domination generally? Kingbronco58: I’m here for a revenge game narrative, so I’d love to see Zach Allen pop off against his former team. He has been one of the Broncos’ best free agent signings in recent memory. Allen has been so dominant the last few years that it really opens up opportunities for his teammates. We saw this last week against Seattle where he had three offensive linemen focused on blocking him. Allen will get some pressures, but expect his teammates to be the main beneficiaries. And I think Allen’s pressures will force Brissett into at least one turnover in this game. MHR – Payton assured fans the Broncos would not overlook the Cardinals as the rematch with the Chiefs is looming. What would show you in this upcoming game that the Broncos are better suited to take on the Chiefs next week than in their first meeting Week 1? What would concern you? Kingbronco58: Better tackling. Week 1 was a disaster, not only because the offense stunk but because the defense had one of the worst tackling performances in NFL history. The other thing that I’d like to see is the offense to start finding its groove. The Chiefs defense is way more talented than the Cardinals. If we can’t run up the score on the Cardinals, then next week’s best case scenario is a defensive slugfest. “I have to play better. We have to play better. The offense has to play better… We’re going to be just fine.” Broncos QB Bo Nix focused on individual and team improvement ahead of #DENvsAZ » https://t.co/5yoZ7LzLge pic.twitter.com/XWiFvQ9Kt5 — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) October 21, 2026 Predictions Stats for BO NIX? 19/27, 274yds, 2 TDs Stats for each Broncos RB? Dobbins 14 carries 53 yds, Harvey 5 carries 24 yds, Coleman 6 carries 32 yds 1 TD Number of yards receiving/TDs for the receivers? I’m going to this game, and this will be 5th time watching the Broncos on the road. I’m 0-4… but of course I’m going to predict that I get to witness my first road win this Sunday! teamStories.summary: Edge rusher, center are leaders in the trenches and elevated performances goes a long way if Las Vegas wants to win
teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images A get-right game for the Las Vegas Raiders? These types don’t come often for the Silver & Black but that’s what the Week 7 home date with the Los Angeles Rams is shaping up to be. Pegged as a “super team”, the visiting Rams have been anything but that. Sean McVay’s squad is 2-4 overall and riding a two-game losing skid which began with a Week 5 37-34 overtime loss to the Buffalo Bills. That was followed by an 18-16 defeat to the Arizona Cardinals last Sunday. And now the offensive genius that McVay is contends with a roster decimated by injuries. L.A. will be limping into this matchup having lost key contributors in Week 6 to injury, such as wide receiver Davante Adams (hamstring), defensive tackles Kobie Turner (groin) and Poona Ford (ruptured triceps), and kicker Blake Grupe (torn ACL). In addition to that, the Rams will be without standout linebacker Nate Landman (concussion) in their outing in Las Vegas. Full #Rams injuries from Week 6: – WR Davante Adams – ruptured hamstring, out 6-10 weeks – DT Kobie Turner – groin, out 4-6 weeks – DT Poona Ford – ruptured triceps, out for season – K Blake Grupe – torn ACL, out for season Also: Myles Garrett isn't ready to come back and is… pic.twitter.com/wJFSAU46qu — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) October 19, 2026 It’s a perfect storm of a get-right opportunity for the 3-3 Raiders to get back in the win column as their galivanting on a three-game losing streak. And in order to rid themselves of consecutive losses and take advantage of a silver nugget in front of them, Klint Kubiak’s desert marauders need elevated play from certain players: Such as edge rusher Maxx Crosby and center Tyler Linderbaum. Football often begins and ends in the trenches and both represent elite talent at their respective positions on Las Vegas defensive and offensive lines. It’s almost blasphemy to say Crosby needs to step up considering his uncanny stamina and will but not even that non-stop motor or sheer determination is lighting up the stat sheet like it used to. The 29-year-old 6-foot-5 and 255-pound edge rusher is off to the slowest start of his career when it comes to finishing plays behind the line of scrimmage. Crosby remains a harrier for quarterbacks and is among league leaders in pressures through the first six games, however, he only has two sacks on the year and also only two tackles for loss. At this current rate, the Raiders elite pass rusher is on pace to rack up just five sacks (his career low was seven in his second season in the NFL in 2020) and five to seven tackles for loss (career low was 13 in 2021). These are two categories where Crosby tends to go ham in the box score. Maxx volume 🔊 Don't miss an all-new Mic'd Up with Maxx Crosby LIVE NOW! 📺: https://t.co/bddAGwCPtg pic.twitter.com/6JKTB3uWcN — Las Vegas Raiders (@Raiders) October 22, 2026 Not only pressuring but hitting or taking down Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford is a must-do this Sunday for the Raiders and it’s Crosby who leads that charge. According to Pro Football Reference, Crosby is charted with 24 pressures, 11 hurries, and 10 hits on the quarterback. Those pressure numbers are impressive considering PFR charted Crosby with 29 total pressures last season — one in which he had 10 sacks. Crosby hasn’t received much help from his fellow defensive linemen in the sack department, however. And elevated play from defensive tackles Adam Butler, Folorunso Fatukasi, and the returning Tonka Hemingway (concussion) will be tremendous for getting interior pressure on Stafford — whose arm powers the Rams top-ranked and second-ranked passing game in terms of attempts and yards gained. Flip the trenches to the offensive side of the ball, Las Vegas needs improved play at the pivot from Linderbaum. The high-priced free agent acquisition was rag dolled by Buffalo Bills defensive tackle Deone Walker in last week’s matchup and the Raiders can ill-afford to have that happen anymore. Getting manhandled at the point of attack hurt Las Vegas run game and offensive line as a whole, but Linderbaum appears ready to showcase Week 6’s performance was the outlier. And this brings us to the ground game — the aspect of the Raiders offense that continues to struggle despite the concentrated effort the team has done to improve upon it. “Yeah, I think the common theme is myself. We got to be better as coaches at getting our guys in the best situation, and just keep improving. And that starts on the practice field,” Kubiak said during his media session on Friday. “So, this time of year, when guys start getting a little bit dinged up, some of the reps go down a little bit, so just being really intentional about what reps you give them versus what fronts, so we can give them a good picture of what to expect in the game.” Tyler Linderbaum talks about the team's response this week as the #Raiders look to improve the run game against the LA Rams on Sunday pic.twitter.com/fymaeO4yPk — Raider Nation Radio (@RNR920AM) October 22, 2026 Improved execution by the front five on the offensive line and quick decision-making by running backs Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington Jr. is integral if Las Vegas intends to topple Los Angeles. While the Raiders run game may boast the third-worst group in the NFL (475 yards rushing), the Rams run defense allows seventh most rushing yards (762). Facing a Rams team without two key defensive tackles and the stud linebacker should help the Silver & Black, too. “Yeah, guys, we just got to go do it. Got to quit talking about it, and we got to go do it,” Kubiak said when asked how close his team is to finding a groove running the ball. Even with a struggling ground game, Kubiak and veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins lead the NFL’s seventh-most productive aerial attack (1,581 yards) and Las Vegas has the second-most passing touchdowns (14) in the league. Cousins is completing 63.4 percent of his passes with a league-leading 14 touchdowns (and just five interceptions). He’s only been sacked eight times and if the offensive line and ground game are clicking, it should further open up the array of artillery Kubiak dials up. Heightened effort and execution form tight end Brock Bowers and speedy wide receiver Tre Tucker can make the Raiders top two pass catchers (28 receptions, 382 yards, three touchdowns and 24 receptions, 371 yards, three touchdowns, respectively) even more dangerous in this home clash with the Rams.

teamStories.title: Former Raiders RB Pete Banaszak dies at 82
teamStories.summary: Former Raiders running back Pete Banaszak has died, the team announced Saturday.
teamStories.detailText: Former Raiders running back Pete Banaszak has died, the team announced Saturday. He was 82. "The Raiders Family mourns the passing of Pete Banaszak, whose toughness, competitive spirit, and dedication embodied a legendary era of Raiders football and made him a cherished member of the Silver and Black," the team said in a statement. "The deepest condolences of the entire Raider Nation are with Pete's wife Sue, daughters Rebecca and Amy, grandsons Luke, Austin, and Connor, and all of his loved ones." Banaszak played his entire career with the Raiders. The team drafted him in the fifth round of the 1966 AFL Draft, and he retired after the 1978 season. He led the NFL with 16 rushing touchdowns in 1975, which remains a single-season franchise record. He won a Super Bowl XI ring, which was the franchise's first Super Bowl championship. Banaszak appeared in 173 regular-season games with the Raiders and played a central role in the famous "Holy Roller" play. Banaszak, a Wisconsin native, was inducted into the National Polish-American Sports Hall of Fame in 1990.

teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders are gearing up for what feels like a “must-win” game in Week 7 against the hobbled Los Angeles Rams . However, the NFL Trade Deadline is quickly approaching (Tuesday, Nov. 10 at 1 p.m. PST), and that’s the biggest focus of this week’s mailbag. So, let’s get to it! Q: What players would be good options for the Raiders’ timeline to buy at the trade deadline? A: Understandably, I got a bunch of questions about Quenton Nelson, so I’ll dive into my thoughts on him in the question/answer below and focus on other players here, all of whom come from The Athletic’s big board . Shout out to Daniel Popper for putting that together! DT Jeffery Simmons, Tennessee Titans Normally, I wouldn’t be in favor of trading for someone who will turn 30 in the summer. But 2025 was Simmons’ best season, and he’s been playing well this year, so it’s not as if he’s showing signs of regressing. Also, he signed an extension in the offseason and would be under team control through 2030. The issue with Simmons to the Raiders is that he was arrested for violence against a woman, and Mark Davis typically draws the line there. However, the incident occurred when Simmons was still in high school and was over a decade ago, and he hasn’t been in any legal trouble since then. DT Moro Ojomo, Philadelphia Eagles Ojomo is an impending free agent, so trading for him would also require a contract extension. The other end of that is that John Spytek could wait until the offseason and just sign Ojomo in free agency without having to give up a draft pick for him. So, it’s just a matter of how much it’s worth to get ahead of the 25-year-old’s market and add a player who would fill the defense’s biggest hole right now to help keep this season afloat? And of course, what the Eagles are willing to accept to part with Ojomo. If Ojomo isn’t traded, there’s a good chance he hits the open market since Philly recently paid defensive tackles Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis. WR Brian Thomas Jr., Jacksonville Jaguars I’ve been pounding this drum for a while. Obviously, Thomas’ production has been underwhelming since his near 1,300-yard performance as a rookie. Otherwise, we wouldn’t be talking about him as a trade candidate. But I get the feeling that’s a relationship issue with Liam Coen. It feels like they’ve never been on the same page and have been butting heads since Coen got the job last year. So, if it’s pennies on the dollar, trading for a 24-year-old who could solve the WR1 problem might be worth the risk. With the fifth-year option, the Raiders could get two-and-a-half seasons to see how Thomas performs in Klint Kubiak’s offense before giving him a big-money extension. G Landon Dickerson, Philadelphia Eagles Buyer beware with Dickerson because he’s had several significant injuries, dating back to his college days. The recent ones seem to have really impacted his play on the field, too. However, when healthy, the three-time Pro Bowler is a very good guard and just turned 28 years old. It’s just a matter of how much risk Spytek and Co. are willing to take because last season wasn’t pretty for Dickerson, and he’s only played in one game so far this year. Q: Should the Raiders give up a 2nd and 4th along with a player to get Quenton Nelson? I may be delusional, but I think this offense could get close to elite with a dominant guard. They need to get the run game fixed, especially when Mendoza takes over. A: I don’t hate the idea of trading for Nelson at all! He’s been a Pro Bowler literally every year of his career, made three first-team All-Pro teams and three more second-team selections, and is playing well this year. Clearly, Nelson would be a MASSIVE upgrade over what the Raiders currently have at guard. But where I get a little pause is that he turns 31 in March and is in a contract year. That makes me more cost-conscious when it comes to a trade. To be clear, I’m not as worried about an offensive lineman’s age since the organization has to protect its investment in Mendoza, especially with a lineman of Nelson’s caliber. But Spytek does have to factor in that the team might only get two or three really good years from Nelson, which impacts how high of a pick he should be willing to give up. Also impacting the price tag or Spytek’s willingness to get a deal done now is that Nelson might be available on the open market this offseason, anyway. It’s the same logic as Ojomo above: How much is getting ahead of the market worth? I wish I had an answer to that question, but there’s only one person who does… For me, second- and fourth-round picks AND a player would be too much. If it’s just a second, I think the Raiders should do that in a heartbeat. They aren’t finding a guard who is even close to as good as Nelson is on Day 2 of the draft. I start to waver when two picks are involved because that’s two players who could get second contracts in Las Vegas when Nelson is likely going to be a one-contract addition. Also, that’s where the fact he might be available in free agency for no draft picks really weighs on my mind. Ultimately, I think Nelson should be on the table for the Raiders, where Spytek is at least picking up the phone and giving the Colts a call. Q: Trench Questions: How do you feel about the DTs so far this year? We clamored for a true nose tackle in the draft and got next to nothing. Anyone you’re impressed with on our roster? Is there a trade candidate you feel like could provide what we need? A: I touched on a lot of this above, but defensive tackle is by far the weakest position group on the Raiders’ defense right now. Thomas Booker IV is probably having the best season of the position group, and Booker is nothing to write home about. If Spytek doesn’t trade for one of the two defensive tackles mentioned above — and you could throw Vita Vea in there, too — then it needs to be one of the general manager’s top priorities in the offseason. He’s ignored it for too long and the defense is paying the price. The draft class has been pretty disapointing at the position as a whole this year, but I still really like Ole Miss’ Will Echoles and Tennesssee’s Xavier Gilliam has been a huge riser this season. In free agency, I’ll be keeping my eye on Ojomo and Kobie Turner from the Los Angeles Rams to give you a few names to keep tabs on for the offseason. Q: Chances of seeing Jackson Powers-Johnson or Trey Zuhn III start at LG? I’m not mad at Caleb Rogers getting live reps at RG if they see him as a future long-term RG. I’m sure Burford isn’t the long-term answer at LG. A: I get the feeling Powers-Johnson’s days in Las Vegas are numbered. It hasn’t been a big deal this year because I think he realized after the Raiders gave Tyler Linderbaum a bag in free agency that his only chance at seeing the field is at guard, but JPJ made it no secret during his first two years that he wants to play center. Now that he’s not even starting at guard, I can see a “mutual parting of ways” coming in the future. Maybe not at the deadline, but that will at least be a talking point in the offseason. I view this as a similar situation to Tyree Wilson this past offseason. Zuhn, on the other hand, I could absolutely see starting at left guard at some point this season. As you mentioned, Burford played well last week after getting called out in the media ( you’re welcome, Spencer! ), but he’s been far from consistent this season and throughout his career. Also, he’s only on a one-year contract while Zuhn is in year one of a third-round rookie contract, giving the latter a lot more future/long-term value. When does that happen? Well, your guess is as good as mine because, in my opinion, Klint Kubiak is too attached to Burford. But if the veteran doesn’t start stringing good games together, the rookie is waiting in the wings, and Kubiak might get forced to make that change. Q: Do you think the Eagles still think they’re SB contenders and might make an unreasonable offer for a 1-year Kirk Cousins rental? Really happy to have Mendoza sit and learn and think Cousins has done good work for us… but I wouldn’t hate an unreasonable offer either. A: I get the feeling that the Eagles are okay with punting on this season. They’ve had a bunch of turmoil between significant injuries, Lane Johnson retiring and now the whole Jalen Hurts blood clots debacle, so I think they’re willing to just take the rest of the season in stride. Also, I don’t think they’re a quarterback away from becoming a legitimate Super Bowl contender again, especially one who comes in midseason and has to learn a new playbook and whatnot. Also, I think having Cousins around while Mendoza is starting would be valuable for the Raiders. Whenever he takes over, Mendoza is going to have his ups and downs as a starter. That’s where having a mentor like Cousins helps because it gives the rookie a peer to talk to when it comes to staying mentally resilient in the NFL, especially since Cousins has been through the wringer during his 15 years in the league. Q: If the Raiders lose 3 of their next 4 games, will there be several trades to acquire draft picks, given their needs & only 5 picks? A: A couple of clarifications here before I dive into the answer. The trade deadline is the Tuesday after Week 9, so it’d have to be two of the next three games instead of three of four. Also, the Raiders have seven picks in the 2027 draft, according to Sumer Sports . One in each of the first five rounds, two in the sixth and none in the seventh. But your point still holds that they could fall significantly out of playoff contention over the next few weeks and could use some more draft picks. The problem is that, in general, the NFL has the least active trade deadline of any professional sport, given how much more important learning/mastering the playbook and chemistry with teammates are in football compared to basketball or baseball. So, I don’t think there would be “several” trades from Las Vegas at the deadline, but one or two could be realistic if the team’s playoff hopes are slipping. Also, if Spytek is waiting to see how the next three weeks go before making a trade, it’s going to be hard to get multiple deals done in two days. He’d have to start negotiating a week or two before and be transparent with the other GMs that any deal is contingent on the Raiders’ record, and I could see the other GMs not wanting to put in all the legwork to agree to deals that might not even happen. And if Spytek isn’t transparent, then he risks pissing off his counterparts and getting a reputation as someone who doesn’t negotiate in good faith, making it difficult to pull off trades in the future. Q: This week I want to focus on one: Michael Richard Mayer. Let’s face it, this guy was “meh” to most of the fanbase and did nothing to cement himself as a good TE. Then Kubiak comes along, and all of a sudden that extension Mayer got makes sense. Good player, schemed right, or combination of both? A: It’s definitely a combination of both. For one, Mayer has been healthy, both physically and mentally, and that was an issue during his first three years after missing 13 games during that timeframe. He’s always been super talented; widely considered one of, if not the, best tight ends in the 2023 draft class, which was really strong at the position. Finally being able to stay on the field (so far) has definitely helped with Mayer’s development. Additionally, Kubiak has done a great job of finding ways to take advantage of his YAC skills. For context, he has the fourth-most yards after the catch (158) among tight ends this season, per Pro Football Focus , and is only 15 yards behind Hunter Henry — who has already played this week — for second place. Also, it helps that Cousins is quick to check the ball down, and Mayer has proven to be a reliable checkdown option. Q: Hey Matt, given the contract extension (deserved imo) to Mike Mayer, what kind of money and contract particulars — length, etc. — would Brock Bowers command? IMO, anything he wants, thanks. View Link A: Someone who knows AI/photoshop better than I do (which is little to nothing) put Bowers’ bald head on Scrooge McDuck’s in the GIF above because that’s going to be him when he gets a contract extension. Right now, George Kittle (4 years, $76.4 million or $19.1 million per year) and Trey McBride (4 years, $76 million or $19 million per year) are the highest-paid tight ends in the NFL. Bowers is going to crush that and probably get wide receiver money. Especially with how Kubiak has been using him, the Raiders are going to find themselves in a similar situation as the Saints did with Jimmy Graham several years ago, where Graham was technically a tight end but used more like a wide receiver, leading to some negotiation holdup. It wouldn’t surprise me at all if Bowers gets something similar to Amon-Ra St. Brown’s four-year, $120 million contract extension. This past offseason, John Spytek showed that he’s willing to disrupt the market for a young player that he believes is a top-tier talent, making Tyler Linderbaum the league’s highest-paid center by $9 million per year. That sets a precedent, so I don’t see Spytek being cheap when it comes to the offense’s clear best player. Q: Are there any players you would consider extending during the season, as Mayer was? A: Since the Raiders have to wait until the offseason for a Bowers extension, I think Tre Tucker is the only early extension candidate. Maybe Jeremy Chinn falls into that category too. But I don’t think they would be devastated if either of those guys walked in free agency, which should reduce the urgency. At this stage, I’d be kind of surprised if anyone else gets an extension before February. Then again, I didn’t think Mayer would get an early extension, so I won’t close the door on the topic. If Tucker starts stringing a few more productive games together, that will change my perspective. Q: With all the inquiries we’ve seen in the first six weeks alone, would you support adding an 18th game to the season next year and do you think adding a second bye week for each team would make it more palatable? A: I’m not a fan of the 17-game schedule, to be honest. Don’t get me wrong, nobody loves watching good football more than I do, but we didn’t get that in Week 18 last year. There were hardly any meaningful matchups, and look at the Raiders-Chiefs game. That was basically a preseason game where both teams played two quarterbacks, and it was brutal to watch. I just feel like the NFL is toeing the line of losing the novelty of games by expanding the season and adding more games throughout the week. That’s what differentiates it from the NBA, MLB and NHL, where people plan their entire week around Sunday so they can watch football. If the NFL adds more games and/or has a game every night, they’re going to lose some of the scarcity factor. So no, I wouldn’t support the 18-game schedule from that perspective, and the player safety factor that the league likes to tell people they care about while tossing around ideas like this one or expanding the international series despite questionable playing surfaces, etc. But I get the feeling it’s inevitable, and I do think it needs to come with an extra bye week to help reduce the risk of injuries by giving player’s bodies more healing time. Q: I get the o-line issues, but I find it highly disturbing that Ashton Jeanty is not performing that well and that Mike Washington Jr. is performing materially better. A few weeks ago, I wrote it off as a sample size thing or MW hitting a few longer runs. But 34 vs. 98 carries is starting to feel like a more valid sample size, and, well, Jeanty can hit longer runs too, can’t he? I’ve been a believer but am just starting to worry that maybe Jeanty isn’t it. Valid fear or unfounded? A: The Jeanty-Washington debates/statisical comparison is still missing the fact that defenses are playing the two backs differently. Per Sumer Sports , 41.8% of Jeanty’s carries have come against a heavy box (eight defenders or more) and 53.1% have been against base personnell (seven front defensive linemen and linebackers on the field), leading to 78.9% of his yards coming after contact. Meanwhile, Washington’s figures are 20.6%, 41.8% and 66.1% in the same categories. That’s a big reason why the rookie has been able to break more long runs. That being said, I’ve backed Jeanty a bunch on here, and I’m with you in that my patience is starting to wear thin. I do think he can be a good back in the league, but he needs better blocking, which the Raiders haven’t been able to provide. He clearly isn’t the type of back who can make something out of nothing consistently. To be fair, there are very few running backs who can. But when you’re drafted in the same range as Saquon Barkley and Bijan Robinson, that becomes an expectation. For the record, I never thought Jeanty was in that category and is a tier below it. In other words, worthy of a first-round pick but outside of the top 10. I didn’t even do a breakdown on him ahead of the draft because of that and never felt that the Raiders were in a position to draft a running back sixth overall. I promise I’m not trying to pat myself on the back here, I’m just saying we’re seeing the effects of that unfold over the last year and a half. All of this is to say; if there’s an opportunity to trade Jeanty either at the deadline or in the offseason and recoup some value, like a second-rounder, I think the Raiders should jump on that unless something changes in the coming weeks. I’m still not convinced Washington can be a lead back, but adding an extra draft pick to fill another hole while still having someone who can tote the rock would be hard to pass up. That’ll do it for this week’s mailbag. Thank you all for submitting questions and, as your weekly reminder, if you’d like to have your questions answered in a future column, tweet them at me, @MHolder95 , email them to SBPQuestions1@gmail.com or look for our weekly call for questions on the site. The latter will continue to publish on Thursdays.
